title: E-Readers vs Tablets: Which Is Better for Reading?
excerpt: E-readers are light on the eyes and last for weeks; tablets do far more. Compare screens, battery, and price to find your better reading device.
body_html:
If you read every day, the device you read on shapes the habit. E-readers and tablets both hold thousands of books, but they are built for different jobs. An e-reader does one thing, reading, and does it with a screen that feels like paper. A tablet does almost everything, from email to video, and reading is just one of its many talents. Choosing between them comes down to how you read, where you read, and whether you want a dedicated device or a multitasker.

The biggest difference is the screen. Most e-readers use e-ink, which reflects light like paper instead of shining it into your eyes. That makes long reading sessions comfortable, and the battery lasts for weeks rather than hours. Tablets use bright LCD or OLED screens that look great for video and colour, but can tire your eyes after a long chapter. If you compare devices by their screens, our guide to tablets vs laptops: which one fits your daily work explains how screen size and weight affect everyday use.

Where Tablets Win

Tablets win on versatility. You can read a novel, check a recipe, watch a video, and reply to a message without switching devices. Colour illustrations, comics, magazines, and PDFs all look better on a tablet, and a larger screen suits textbooks with diagrams. Tablets also sync easily with the apps you already use, from note-taking to audiobooks. The trade-off is distraction: notifications and other apps sit one tap away, which is exactly what an e-reader removes. Tablets also handle borrowed library books, magazines, and study PDFs without fuss, and a stylus turns one into a notebook for marking up pages. If you travel light, a tablet can replace a laptop for short trips, which is something no e-reader can do.

Price, Weight, and the Verdict

E-readers are usually cheaper, lighter, and easier to hold one-handed on a crowded train. A basic model costs far less than a tablet and survives a drop into a bag without a second thought. Tablets cost more, but they replace several gadgets at once, which can make them better value if you need one device for everything. Our round-up of the best budget gadgets for remote work 2026 shows how to weigh price against what a device actually does for you. If reading is your main hobby, buy the e-reader. If you want one screen for work and play, the tablet is the better buy.

title: How to Write a Better Email That Gets Answered
excerpt: Busy people skim, so a good email is short, clear, and easy to answer. Learn how to write subject lines and messages that actually get replies.
body_html:
Most emails fail before they are even read. The recipient sees a vague subject line, opens a long wall of text, and decides to deal with it later, which usually means never. A good email respects the reader's time. It says what you want in the first two lines, keeps the rest short, and makes replying easy. Whether you are asking a favour, following up on a job, or writing to a customer, the same rules apply: be clear, be brief, and make the next step obvious.

Start with the subject line, because it decides whether your email gets opened at all. A good subject is specific and honest: 'Question about Friday's delivery' beats 'Hello' or 'Quick question' every time. Then put your main point in the opening sentence. Do not bury the request in the third paragraph. If you need background, add it after the ask, not before. Busy people skim, so short paragraphs and one idea per email make your message far easier to answer. If the email is long, add a one-line summary at the top so the reader knows the point before they start. Most people decide in seconds whether to read on.

Structure That Gets Replies

Keep the body to a few short paragraphs and use plain language. One clear request per email works better than three questions tangled together, because the reader can answer in a sentence and move on. If you need research before writing, our guide to how to research any topic online in under an hour shows how to gather facts quickly, so your email sounds informed instead of vague. End with a simple call to action, such as a question or a suggested time, and say when you need an answer. 'Could you confirm by Thursday?' gives the reader a deadline without sounding pushy.

Tone, Timing, and Follow-Ups

Match your tone to the relationship. A short, friendly email suits a colleague you know well; a formal note suits a first contact. Always re-read before sending, and check names, dates, and attachments. If you do not hear back in a few days, send one polite follow-up rather than the same email again. A cluttered inbox makes replies even harder, so keeping yours organised helps too, and our tips on how to clean up your inbox and find any email are a good place to start. Write less, say it sooner, and your emails will start getting answered.

title: Best Free Screen Recording Tools for Tutorials and Work
excerpt: You do not need paid software to record your screen. These free tools capture tutorials, meetings, and demos with surprising quality.
body_html:
Screen recording has become an everyday skill. Teachers record lessons, teams capture bug reports, and anyone can turn a complicated process into a short video that explains itself. You do not need expensive software to do it well. Free tools now record your screen, your voice, and your webcam at the same time, and several are built into the devices you already own. The trick is picking the right tool for the job, because each one suits a different kind of recording.

Start with what you already have. Windows has the Snipping Tool and Game Bar, Mac has Screenshot with screen recording built in, and both handle simple captures without any download. These are perfect for quick clips, such as showing a colleague where to click. For longer tutorials, look for a free recorder that adds annotations, a webcam overlay, and simple editing. If your recording needs polish afterwards, our guide to the best free video editing tools for short clips and reels shows free editors that can trim and tidy the result.

What to Look For in a Free Recorder

Check four things before you choose. First, the time limit: some free tools cap recordings at five or fifteen minutes, which is fine for a bug report but not for a lesson. Second, watermarks, which some free versions stamp on your video. Third, audio options, because a tutorial without clear voiceover is hard to follow. And fourth, the export format, since MP4 works almost everywhere. Record a short test first, watch it back, and check that your voice is clear and the text on screen is readable. Also check where the files are saved and how large they get, because uncompressed recordings can fill a hard drive fast. A five-minute 1080p clip is usually a few hundred megabytes, which is easy to share but worth knowing before you record an hour-long lesson.

Recording Tips That Make a Difference

Good recordings are planned, not improvised. Write down the three or four steps you will show, close unrelated tabs and notifications, and do a quick practice run. Speak slowly and pause between steps so viewers can follow along. If you record meetings, tell everyone first and share the video afterwards, and our comparison of the best free video calling apps for meetings and family can help you pick a calling tool with recording built in. Keep videos short, cut the mistakes, and your tutorials will look far more professional than their price suggests.

title: How to Secure Your Smart Home Devices from Hackers
excerpt: Smart speakers, cameras, and locks connect your home to the internet, and to attackers. Secure them with these simple steps before it is too late.
body_html:
Smart speakers, cameras, doorbells, and locks make life easier, but each one is also a small computer connected to the internet. That connection is what makes them useful, and it is also what makes them a target. Attackers do not need to break into your house when they can guess a weak password, exploit an old device, or slip in through a forgotten account. Securing your smart home is mostly a set of small habits, and most of them take only a few minutes each.

Start with passwords. Many smart devices ship with a default password like 'admin', and many owners never change it. Give every device its own strong password and store them in a password manager. Next, turn on two-factor authentication wherever it is offered, because it blocks most account takeovers even if a password leaks. Our guide to two-factor authentication explained: turn it on in 5 minutes walks through the setup for the accounts that matter most.

Update, Separate, and Switch Off

Outdated software is the most common way attackers get in, so turn on automatic updates for every device and its app. If a device stops receiving updates, consider replacing it, because an unpatched camera or lock is a permanent open door. Put smart devices on a separate Wi-Fi network from your computers and phones if your router supports it, so a compromised bulb cannot reach your laptop. And switch off features you never use, such as remote access or voice purchasing, since every feature you disable is one less way in. Also give your smart home its own email address and password where possible, separate from the account you use for banking or work. If one account is ever exposed, the damage stays contained. Check the maker's website once a year to confirm the device still gets security updates.

Check What You Own

Once a month, take five minutes to review your smart home. Open each app and look for devices you do not recognise, logins from places you have never been, and old accounts you no longer use. Remove anything unfamiliar and change the password. If you suspect a password has already leaked, our guide on how to check if your password has leaked online shows how to find out quickly. A smart home should make you feel safer, not watched, and a little regular attention keeps it that way for years to come, not just today.

title: How to Do a Simple SEO Audit of Your Own Website
excerpt: An SEO audit sounds technical, but a simple check takes under an hour. Walk through your pages, speed, and links to find quick wins.
body_html:
An SEO audit sounds like a job for an expert with expensive software, but a simple check of your own website takes less than an hour and finds most of the easy wins. You are looking for the basics: pages that search engines cannot reach, pages that load slowly, and pages that give visitors no reason to stay. You do not need to fix everything at once. The point of an audit is to make a short list of problems, ordered by impact, so you know what to do first.

Start with a crawl of your own site. Free tools like Screaming Frog's free version or Google Search Console will list your pages and flag the obvious problems: broken links, missing titles, and pages that return errors. Open your homepage and a few key pages in a browser and look at them as a visitor would. Is it clear what each page is about in the first few seconds? If not, note it down. A quick look at your site's speed matters too, and our guide to site speed and Core Web Vitals: why fast pages rank explains what to measure.

Check Content, Titles, and Links

Next, check the content itself. Every page should target one clear topic, with a descriptive title and a heading that matches what people search for. Look for duplicate titles, pages with almost no text, and old posts that no longer match what you offer. Then check your internal links: does every important page receive links from other pages on your site, or are some pages stranded with no way in? Fixing a stranded page can be as simple as adding one link from a related article. Also check that your pages work well on a phone, since most visitors arrive on mobile. Text should be readable without zooming, and buttons should be easy to tap.

Turn Findings Into a Fix List

Finish by writing down everything you found, then sort the list by impact. Broken pages and missing titles come first, because they cost you visitors today. Speed fixes and content updates come next. Set a date to repeat the audit every few months, because websites drift: links break, content ages, and new pages arrive without titles. If your business serves local customers, add the local checks from our guide to local SEO basics: help nearby customers find your business. A regular audit keeps small problems small.

title: What Is RAG? How AI Chatbots Find Facts Before They Answer
excerpt: RAG lets chatbots look up facts before answering, instead of guessing from memory. Here is how retrieval-augmented generation works, simply.
body_html:
AI chatbots are impressive, but they have a famous weakness: they sometimes invent facts with total confidence. The reason is simple. A chatbot answers from patterns it learned during training, not from a library it can check. Retrieval-augmented generation, usually shortened to RAG, fixes this by giving the chatbot a library to consult. Before it answers, the system searches trusted documents, pulls out the relevant passages, and writes its reply using those facts. The result is an answer grounded in real sources rather than memory alone.

RAG works in three steps. First, your documents are split into small chunks and stored in a searchable index. Second, when you ask a question, the system finds the chunks most similar to your question. Third, those chunks are handed to the chatbot along with your question, so it can quote and summarise them. This is similar to how AI deep research tools let the chatbot do the digging, except RAG searches your own documents instead of the whole web.

Why RAG Answers Are More Reliable

Because RAG answers come from documents you can inspect, they are easier to check and easier to trust. If a company builds a support chatbot with RAG, it answers from the company's own help pages, not from a guess. When the documents change, the answers change too, without retraining the whole model. RAG also reduces the odd, confident errors that make chatbots unreliable for anything factual. It is not perfect: if the search finds the wrong documents, the answer can still go wrong, but at least you can see which sources it used. Good RAG systems also show their sources next to the answer, so you can click through and check the original document yourself. That transparency is what turns a clever reply into one you can act on.

Where You Already Meet RAG

You have probably used RAG without knowing it. Customer support bots that quote help articles, search tools that answer with citations, and research assistants that summarise your uploaded files all use the same idea. Even the AI overviews in search results work this way, pulling facts from pages before writing a summary. Our explainer on AI overviews: what they mean for websites and readers shows how that changes what you see at the top of a search page. As chatbots move from clever conversation into real work, the ones that check their facts first are the ones worth trusting.

title: Smart Speakers in 2027: Are They Still Worth Buying?
excerpt: Smart speakers promised a hands-free home, but in 2027 the market looks different. Here is when they are still worth buying — and when to skip one.
body_html:
Smart speakers were once the must-have gadget in every living room. Ask for the weather, play a song, set a timer, turn off the lights — all without lifting a finger. In 2027, though, the excitement has cooled. Sales have flattened, some models have been discontinued, and many people wonder whether the speaker on their shelf is still worth replacing when it finally gives up.

The honest answer is that smart speakers are no longer revolutionary, but they are far from useless. The technology has matured into something quieter and more practical. Voice assistants understand everyday requests better than ever, and the best speakers now sound genuinely good for music.

Where Smart Speakers Still Make Sense

The strongest case is the kitchen, the bedroom, or any room where your hands are busy. A voice-controlled timer while you cook, a gentle alarm that fades in with music, or a quick question answered while you get dressed — these small moments add up. They also work well as a simple hub for a smart home, letting you switch off lights or check a door lock with a single sentence. If you already own compatible lights and plugs, a speaker ties the whole setup together, as our look at a smart home starter kit explains.

Sound quality is the other reason to consider one. The compact models of 2027 produce warm, room-filling audio that easily beats a phone speaker, and the larger models can anchor a small living room.

When You Should Skip One

There are good reasons to pass, too. If you rarely use voice commands, a smart speaker is just an ordinary speaker with a microphone you never use. Privacy is another concern: the device listens for a wake word around the clock, and some people simply prefer not to have that in their home. There is also the question of support — older models lose new features over time, and a speaker tied to one assistant locks you into that ecosystem.

Before you buy, check which assistant your other devices already use, and whether the speaker works with your music service. Read the privacy settings and learn how to delete your voice history. If you mostly want a wearable that answers questions on the move, our guide to wearable tech in 2026 may suit you better. In short, smart speakers in 2027 are worth buying when you have a clear job for them — a kitchen helper, a bedroom alarm, or a music speaker — and not worth buying as a gadget for its own sake.

title: How to Use Google Maps Offline and Never Get Lost
excerpt: No signal does not have to mean no directions. Download a map before you travel and Google Maps will still guide you and find places offline.
body_html:
Losing your mobile signal in an unfamiliar place is stressful. The road signs make no sense, your data has vanished, and the map on your phone is a blank grey grid. It happens on country roads, in underground car parks, on mountain trails, and in foreign cities where roaming costs a fortune. The good news is that you can prepare for it in about two minutes: Google Maps lets you download whole areas to your phone in advance, so navigation keeps working even with no connection at all.

An offline map is simply a saved copy of the map data for one area — streets, place names, and points of interest — stored on your device. Once it is downloaded, your phone uses GPS, which works without mobile data, to show your position and guide you turn by turn.

Download a Map Before You Go

Open Google Maps while you still have Wi-Fi, tap your profile picture, and choose Offline maps. Tap Select your own map, then pinch and drag the box to cover the area you need — a city centre, a national park, or the whole route to your hotel. Give it a clear name, such as the city and the dates of your trip, and let it download over Wi-Fi.

Downloaded maps usually last for about a year, and Google Maps can update them automatically when you are on Wi-Fi. This pairs well with planning ahead: our guide on how to plan a trip with search tools shows how to research a destination before you leave.

What Works Offline — and What Does Not

With a downloaded map you can search for addresses and saved places, get driving directions, and follow turn-by-turn navigation. That covers the situations that matter most when you are lost. A few features need the internet, though: live traffic, public transport timetables, and walking or cycling routes are not available offline, and business opening hours may be out of date. You can still search for places inside the downloaded area, which is often enough to find a petrol station or a restaurant nearby.

For walking in a city, download the map and save your hotel and key stops as favourites so they appear even offline. If you drive, set your destination before you leave Wi-Fi and keep the phone charged. If you want to sharpen your everyday searching before a trip, our tutorial on how to search Google like a pro will help you find better information faster.

title: Passkeys Explained: The Password-Free Way to Sign In
excerpt: Passkeys replace passwords with your fingerprint or face. They are harder to steal, impossible to phish the usual way, and faster to use every day.
body_html:
Most of us have a love-hate relationship with passwords. We know they should be long and unique, but remembering dozens of them is impossible, so we reuse the same few everywhere. Then a website gets breached, and suddenly that one password opens half our digital life. Passkeys are the industry's answer to this problem: a way to sign in without a password at all. Google, Apple, and Microsoft now support them, and they are quietly becoming the default on new accounts.

A passkey is a pair of digital keys. Your device keeps a private key locked behind your fingerprint, face, or PIN, and the website stores only the matching public key. When you sign in, the site sends a challenge, your device signs it with the private key, and you are in. The private key never leaves your device, so there is nothing useful for a hacker to steal from a breached server.

Why Passkeys Are Safer Than Passwords

The biggest advantage is protection against phishing. A passkey only works on the real website it was created for, so a fake login page cannot trick it into signing in. There is also nothing to guess, reuse, or write on a sticky note. Even if someone watches you type, there is nothing to see — you simply unlock your device with your face or finger.

Passkeys also solve the memory problem completely. You never have to invent, remember, or reset a password again. If you already use a password manager, passkeys fit naturally alongside it — most managers can now store passkeys and sync them between devices. Our roundup of the best password managers in 2026 explains which tools handle passkeys well.

How to Start Using Passkeys

Start with one important account, such as your email or your Google account. Sign in, open the security settings, and look for the option to create a passkey. Your phone or computer will ask you to confirm with your fingerprint or face, and that is it — the passkey is saved. The next time you sign in, you will be offered the passkey instead of a password.

A few practical notes: passkeys sync through your device account, so keep your phone backed up and know your device passcode. If you lose a device, you can remove its passkeys from your account settings, just as you would change a password. Pairing passkeys with cloud backup is smart too — see our comparison of the best free cloud storage for safe places to keep a backup.

title: Ransomware Explained: What It Is and How to Avoid It
excerpt: Ransomware locks your files and demands payment to unlock them. It usually starts with one careless click — but a few simple habits make you a hard target.
body_html:
Ransomware is one of the most feared words in online security, and for good reason. It is malicious software that locks your files — photos, documents, work projects — and then demands a payment, usually in cryptocurrency, to unlock them. Victims often discover it when they sit down to work and find a message on their screen instead of their files. Hospitals, schools, small businesses, and ordinary home users have all been hit. The good news is that ransomware is not magic, and the habits that stop it are simple.

Ransomware usually arrives the same way most malware does: through a phishing email, a malicious download, or a fake software update. One click runs the program, and within minutes it begins encrypting files on your computer and any connected drives. The ransom note then appears, with a deadline and a threat to delete the files or publish them if you do not pay.

How Ransomware Reaches Your Computer

The most common route is email. A message that looks like an invoice, a delivery notice, or a document from a colleague carries an attachment or a link. Opening it starts the infection. The second route is software: outdated programs and operating systems have holes that attackers exploit, often without you clicking anything at all. The third is downloads from unofficial sites — free software, game mods, and pirated files are frequent carriers.

Phishing is the entry point for most attacks, so learning to recognise it matters more than any security product. Our guide on how to spot a phishing email before you click walks through the warning signs, from urgent language to mismatched sender addresses.

Five Habits That Keep You Safe

First, back up your files regularly to a drive you disconnect afterwards, or to a cloud service with version history. A backup turns ransomware from a disaster into an annoyance, because you can wipe the computer and restore everything. Second, keep your operating system and apps updated — updates patch the holes attackers use. Third, use reputable security software and keep it running. Fourth, be careful with email attachments and links, and never enable macros in a document you did not expect.

Fifth, use strong, unique passwords and turn on two-factor authentication, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get in. If the worst happens, do not pay: disconnect the computer from the network, seek professional help, and restore from your backup. If an account is ever compromised, our guide on what to do if your account is hacked walks you through recovery step by step.

title: Featured Snippets and People Also Ask: Win More Search Visibility
excerpt: Featured snippets and People Also Ask boxes put your content above the normal results. Learn how to structure answers so Google picks yours.
body_html:
When you search Google for a question, you often get the answer before you even click a link. A short paragraph sits in a box at the top of the results, sometimes with a list or a table. That is a featured snippet, often called position zero, and just below it you may see a People Also Ask box full of related questions. For websites, these boxes are valuable: they put your content above the traditional number-one result, and they can send a steady stream of visitors to your pages.

The idea is simple. Google wants to answer questions directly, so it looks for pages that answer a specific question clearly and concisely. If your page does that better than everyone else, Google may lift your answer into the snippet.

How to Win a Featured Snippet

Start by finding the exact question people ask. Tools like Google's own People Also Ask box, search suggestions, and keyword research reveal real questions in your topic. Then answer each question on your page in a short, direct paragraph of about forty to sixty words, right after a heading that repeats the question. That paragraph should stand alone: a reader who sees only that text should get a complete answer. Follow it with more detail, examples, or a step-by-step list for readers who want to go deeper.

Use headings that match the question, keep your language plain, and avoid burying the answer under a long introduction. Understanding the question behind the search is the real skill here, and our guide to what search intent is and why it decides your rankings explains how to match your content to what people actually want.

Using People Also Ask to Your Advantage

People Also Ask boxes are more than a source of ideas — they are a map of what your audience is curious about. Open a box, click a question, and more questions appear, each one revealing another gap your content can fill. Add a short FAQ section to your article that answers three or four of these related questions in the same direct style. Each answer is another chance to be picked up as a snippet, and together they show Google that your page covers the topic thoroughly.

A snippet that fully answers a simple question may satisfy the searcher without a visit, so choose questions that naturally lead to a longer read. Combine this with solid page basics — clear titles, descriptive headings, and good meta descriptions — as our on-page SEO checklist explains.

title: AI Shopping Assistants: Can Chatbots Help You Buy Smarter?
excerpt: AI shopping assistants can compare products, summarise reviews, and spot bad deals. They are useful helpers — but they have biases worth knowing.
body_html:
Shopping online used to mean opening a dozen tabs, comparing prices, reading reviews, and hoping you had not missed a better deal. Now a new helper is appearing in that process: the AI shopping assistant. Built into search engines, chatbots, and retailer apps, these assistants promise to find products, compare options, and even warn you about a bad deal — all through a simple conversation. But can a chatbot really help you buy smarter, or is it just another way to sell you things?

An AI shopping assistant works like a knowledgeable shop friend. You describe what you need — a waterproof jacket under a certain price, a laptop for video editing, a gift for a gardener — and it searches product listings, reads reviews, and presents a shortlist. The best ones explain their reasoning: why this model fits your budget, what owners complain about, and where the price has been lower before.

What AI Shopping Assistants Do Well

They are strongest at the boring parts of shopping: gathering options, summarising hundreds of reviews into a few sentences, and spotting patterns you would miss. If a product has a recurring fault mentioned in dozens of reviews, an assistant will usually surface it.

They are also useful for narrowing a huge choice down to three or four serious options. Instead of comparing fifty headphones, you can ask for the best three under a budget with good battery life, then research those properly. Used this way, the assistant is a filter, not a decision-maker. The final choice stays with you, which is exactly how it should be — especially when reviews can be misleading, as our guide on how to tell if a product review is trustworthy explains.

Where You Should Stay Sceptical

The biggest weakness is bias. An assistant may favour products from partner retailers, promote sponsored listings, or simply lack information about a brand it has not indexed. Its knowledge can also be out of date: a price it quotes may have changed, a model may be discontinued, or a new version may have launched.

AI answers can also sound confident while being wrong, inventing a feature or a review that does not exist. That is why a quick fact-check matters before any purchase. Our routine for fact-checking AI answers takes only a minute and catches most errors. Ask the assistant for sources and links, compare its shortlist with one independent review site, and be wary if it pushes a single product very hard.

title: Drones for Beginners: What to Know Before Your First Flight
excerpt: A beginner drone can shoot stunning video for less than a phone costs — but rules, wind, and battery life catch new pilots out. Here is what to know first.
body_html:
Drones have gone from expensive hobbyist toys to affordable flying cameras in less than a decade. A decent beginner drone now costs less than a mid-range phone, shoots steady 4K video, and practically flies itself. But before your first flight, there are a few things worth knowing. A little preparation saves you from a crash, a fine, or a drone stuck in a tree.

The first decision is which drone to buy. For beginners, a small model under 250 grams is usually the best choice. It is lighter, cheaper, and in many countries it faces fewer rules than heavier drones. Look for obstacle avoidance, a return-to-home button, and at least twenty minutes of flight time per battery.

Learn the Rules Before You Fly

Drone rules vary by country, but the basics are similar almost everywhere: do not fly near airports, over crowds, or above a certain height, and keep the drone where you can see it. Many countries require registration for heavier drones, and some require a simple online test. Check your local aviation authority's website before your first flight — it takes ten minutes and keeps you legal.

Privacy matters as well. A camera in the sky can make neighbours uncomfortable, so avoid hovering over gardens and windows. Fly in open spaces, respect other people's privacy, and you will rarely have a problem. If you enjoy photography from the air, our guide to the best cameras for beginners in 2026 covers the basics of framing and light that apply just as well from above.

Your First Flight, Step by Step

Pick a wide open space on a calm day — a large field, a quiet beach, or an empty car park. Wind is a beginner's worst enemy, so avoid gusty days entirely. Charge the battery fully, update the drone's software, and calibrate the compass as the app instructs. Take off slowly, hover at a few metres, and practise moving gently in each direction before you try anything ambitious. Keep your first flights short: fifteen minutes of calm, careful flying teaches more than an hour of panicked chasing.

Bring spare batteries and a landing pad if you have one, and always keep the return-to-home feature in mind — it is your safety net when the battery runs low or you lose your bearings. Drones are a lot like electric scooters: the basics are easy, but a little respect for the machine goes a long way, as our beginners guide to city rides shows for another fun gadget.

title: How to Record a Podcast with Just Your Phone
excerpt: Your phone is already a podcast studio: a mic, a recorder, and an editor in one. Here is how to record, edit, and publish your first episode.
body_html:
You do not need a studio, a mixing desk, or an expensive microphone to start a podcast. The phone in your pocket already has a decent microphone, free recording apps, and enough storage for hours of audio. Thousands of shows began exactly this way, recorded in a bedroom or a parked car. This guide shows you how to get from idea to finished episode with just your phone.

Start with the simplest setup possible: your phone, its built-in voice recorder or a free app, and a pair of wired earphones with a microphone if you have them. The earphone mic sits close to your mouth, which usually sounds better than the phone's speaker mic held at arm's length. Record a one-minute test and listen back with headphones.

Record in a Quiet, Soft Room

Sound quality is mostly about the room, not the device. Hard surfaces bounce sound around and make voices echoey, while soft furnishings absorb it. A bedroom with curtains, a bed, and a wardrobe is often the best studio in the house. Close the windows, turn off noisy appliances, and put your phone on silent — a single notification ping can ruin a good take.

Hold the phone about fifteen centimetres from your mouth, slightly to the side so your breath does not hit the mic directly. Speak at a natural pace and do not worry about small mistakes; you can pause, repeat a sentence, and cut the bad version later. Backing up your audio matters as well — our guide on how to back up your photos and files in 20 minutes shows how to keep your recordings safe.

Edit and Publish From Your Phone

Free apps can handle the whole editing process on your phone: trimming silence, removing mistakes, and adding a short intro. Keep your edits simple at first — cut the obvious errors, leave the natural pauses, and do not over-process the sound. Export as an MP3 and listen to the whole episode once before you publish.

For publishing, free podcast hosts let you upload episodes and distribute them to the major apps from your phone. Write a short description for each episode, choose a clear title, and use a simple square cover image. Consistency matters more than perfection: one episode a week, released on the same day, builds an audience faster than a single polished episode followed by silence. If you want ideas for episode topics, our guide to how to organise your digital notes will help you keep a running list of ideas.

title: Best Budgeting Apps to Track Spending in 2027
excerpt: A budgeting app shows exactly where your money goes, but only if you actually use it. Here is how to pick one that fits your habits — and make it stick.
body_html:
Most of us have no idea where our money actually goes. We check the bank balance, feel vaguely surprised, and promise to be more careful next month. A budgeting app turns that vague feeling into clear numbers: how much you spent on food, transport, and subscriptions, and what is left before payday. The best ones do the tracking automatically, so you only need a few minutes a week to stay in control.

A good budgeting app connects to your bank, categorises your spending, and shows it in simple charts. Some focus on giving every pound or dollar a job before you spend it. Others simply track what you spent and warn you when a category is running hot. Neither approach is better in general — the right one is the one you will actually open.

What to Look For in a Budgeting App

Start with the basics: does it support your bank and your currency, and does it sync automatically? Manual entry sounds fine on day one and becomes a chore by week three. Look for clear category reports, spending alerts, and a way to set monthly limits per category. A shared budget feature matters if you manage money with a partner, and a good search makes it easy to find that one mystery payment.

Price is the other question. Many good apps have a free version that covers the essentials, and paying a small yearly fee is worth it only if you use the extra features, such as bill reminders or shared budgets. Keeping your financial life organised pairs well with keeping your digital life organised: our comparison of the best free note-taking apps can help you keep track of bills, receipts, and money notes in one place.

Make the App Work for You

Once you have picked an app, set it up properly in one sitting. Connect your accounts, tidy the categories, and set realistic limits based on what you actually spent last month — not what you wish you had spent. Check the app once a week for ten minutes: review the categories, move anything miscategorised, and look at the month so far.

After a month you will see patterns: the subscription you forgot, the weekday lunches that add up, the category that always blows its limit. Cancel one unused subscription, set a weekly food budget, or move a small amount to savings on payday. Planning your money also means planning your time: our roundup of the best calendar apps for planning your week helps you schedule the money habits that keep a budget working.

title: How to Delete Old Accounts and Reduce Your Digital Footprint
excerpt: Old accounts you forgot about still hold your data — and each one is a door a breach can open. Here is how to find them, delete them, and stay tidy.
body_html:
Think about how many accounts you have created over the years: old email addresses, shopping sites you used once, forums you joined in 2015, apps you deleted but never closed. Each one holds a piece of your personal data — your name, your email, sometimes your address or payment details. Together they form your digital footprint, and the bigger it is, the more there is to leak, breach, or misuse.

Start by making a list. Search your main email inbox for welcome messages, password resets, and receipts — they are a map of every account you ever created. Your browser's saved passwords and your phone's app history are also good sources. Sort the list into three groups: accounts you still use, accounts you might need, and accounts you can delete today.

Delete in the Right Order

Work through the easy deletions first. Many sites now offer a delete option in the account settings, often under Privacy or Data. If there is no obvious button, search the site's help pages for how to close an account, or use a service that collects direct deletion links. Some accounts require an email to support, and a few will make you wait through a cooling-off period before the data is gone.

Before you delete anything, save what you need: download photos, export contacts, and move any important documents. Check whether the account is linked to other logins — deleting a Google or Apple account you use to sign in elsewhere can lock you out of other services. Our guide on how to check if your password has leaked online is a good companion step: if an old account appears in a breach, delete it sooner rather than later.

Keep Your Footprint Small From Now On

Deleting old accounts is only half the job; the other half is creating fewer new ones. Before signing up for a service, ask whether you really need an account or whether you can check out as a guest. When you must sign up, use a unique email alias or a secondary address so a breach does not expose your main inbox. Turn off marketing emails, remove old payment methods, and review app permissions on your phone every few months.

Set a reminder to repeat this cleanup twice a year — it takes an hour once you have done it the first time. For a broader routine, our online safety checklist for 2027 covers ten habits that keep your digital life tidy and secure.

author: The Edge Search

title: Internal Linking for Beginners: Connect Your Pages for Better Rankings
excerpt: Internal links help readers find more of your content and help search engines understand your site. Here is how to link your pages well.
body_html:
Every page on your website is stronger when it is connected to the rest of your site. Internal links are the links from one page on your site to another page on the same site, and they do two jobs at once. They help readers discover related content without going back to a search engine, and they help search engines understand which pages matter most and how your topics fit together.

Think of your website as a small town. Each page is a building, and internal links are the roads between them. Without roads, visitors can only reach one building at a time and then they leave. With good roads, they wander from page to page, spending more time on your site and finding answers they did not know they needed.

Start With Your Most Important Pages

Begin by listing the pages you most want people and search engines to find, such as your main guides, product pages, or popular articles. These are the pages that should receive the most internal links. Then look for natural places to link to them from your other content. A good link fits the sentence it sits in, so the reader genuinely wants to click it. Before you plan new links, it helps to know what your audience is looking for, and our guide to keyword research for beginners shows how to find topics people actually search for.

Use descriptive anchor text, the clickable words of the link, instead of vague phrases like click here. Anchor text such as guide to on-page SEO tells both readers and search engines what the linked page is about. Aim for a handful of relevant links per article rather than dozens, and check that every link still works when you update old content.

Build Simple Habits That Keep Links Working

Make internal linking part of your publishing routine. Every time you write a new article, add two or three links to older, related pages, and then go back and add a link from one or two older pages to the new one. A short checklist helps here, and our on-page SEO checklist covers titles, headings, and meta descriptions alongside linking basics.

Once a month, spend twenty minutes reviewing your links. Fix any that point to deleted pages, and look for older articles that could link to your newest work. You do not need special tools to start, just a habit of connecting each new page to the pages it relates to. Over time, that web of links turns a collection of separate pages into a site that readers enjoy exploring and search engines can understand.

title: AI Search for Students: Research Papers Without the Guesswork
excerpt: AI search can speed up student research, from finding sources to understanding dense papers. Here is how to use it well and stay accurate.
body_html:
Researching a paper used to mean long evenings in the library, paging through indexes and hoping the right journal was on the shelf. Today, AI search tools can point students to relevant sources, summarise long papers, and explain dense academic language in plain words within minutes.

The trick is to treat AI search as a research assistant, not a source itself. Ask it to find papers on a topic, suggest search terms you had not thought of, or explain a concept before you dive into the original text. Then read the actual papers it points to. Your essay or assignment should be built on real sources you have checked, not on an answer a chatbot produced.

Ask Better Questions to Get Better Sources

Start with a clear, specific question rather than a broad topic. Instead of asking about climate change, ask how coastal cities are adapting to rising sea levels, and mention the angle you need, such as policy, engineering, or economics. Ask the tool to show its sources, and prefer tools that link to published papers, university pages, or reputable journals. When a tool can dig through many sources at once, it is worth learning how it works, as our guide to AI deep research tools explains.

Keep a simple log of what you find: the paper title, the authors, the year, and one sentence about why it matters for your argument. This takes a minute per source and saves hours later when you write your bibliography.

Check Every Claim Before You Cite It

AI tools sometimes invent details, including references that look real but do not exist. Before you cite anything, open the source and confirm the quote, the data, or the finding is really there. Cross-check surprising claims in a second source, and be extra careful with numbers, dates, and statistics. A short fact-checking routine is a useful habit for every student, and the way you phrase your questions changes the quality of the answers, so our guide on how to write better prompts is worth reading before your next research session.

Finally, remember that your lecturer cares about your thinking, not just your sources. Use AI search to understand the material faster, then form your own argument, compare different views, and write in your own words. Cite properly, keep track of where each idea came from, and never paste AI output into your work as if it were your own. Done that way, AI search becomes a genuine study skill: faster research, stronger sources, and a paper you can defend with confidence.

title: Portable Monitors for Laptops: A Bigger Screen Anywhere
excerpt: A portable monitor adds a second screen to your laptop bag. Here is what to look for, what to skip, and how to set one up anywhere.
body_html:
Working on a single laptop screen can feel cramped, especially when you need a document open beside a video call or a spreadsheet next to your notes. A portable monitor solves that problem by adding a second screen that fits in your bag.

The idea is simple, but the details matter. Most portable monitors connect over USB-C, and many draw power from the laptop itself, so there is no extra charger to pack. Older laptops may need a Mini-HDMI cable or a small adapter instead, so check your ports before you buy.

What to Look for Before You Buy

Screen size is the first decision. A fourteen-inch model is light and easy to carry, while a seventeen-inch model gives you more room but adds weight and bulk. Resolution matters too: a Full HD screen is fine for documents and browsing, but a higher resolution looks sharper if you edit photos or video. Brightness is easy to overlook, yet it decides whether the screen is usable near a window or outdoors, so look for at least 300 nits if you work in bright places. If you already have a desk setup, our guide to setting up a second monitor covers the basics of arranging two screens comfortably.

Also check the stand. Some monitors come with a folding cover that doubles as a stand, while others need a separate prop or a small tripod. A wobbly stand gets annoying fast, so read reviews that mention stability. Touchscreen models cost more and are only worth it if you actually tap and swipe on a second screen.

Using a Second Screen on the Go

Once it is connected, arrange the screens in your display settings so the mouse moves naturally between them. Keep your main task on the laptop screen and put reference material, chat, or music on the portable one. Lower the brightness a little when you run on battery, because a second screen drains power faster, and carry the monitor in a padded sleeve to protect it. The screen size and ports of your laptop shape the whole setup, so if you are still choosing a machine, our guide to what to look for before you buy a laptop will help you pick one that pairs well with a portable display.

A portable monitor will not replace a big desk display, but that is not its job. It gives you room to work properly wherever you happen to be, without turning your bag into a suitcase. For students, freelancers, and anyone who works away from a desk, that extra screen is often the single most useful upgrade after the laptop itself.

title: How to Transfer Files Between Phone and Computer Without Cables
excerpt: No cable? No problem. Here are the easiest wireless ways to move photos, documents, and videos between your phone and your computer.
body_html:
Most of us have been there: a photo is on your phone, you need it on your computer, and the cable is in another room, another bag, or lost entirely. The good news is that you rarely need a cable at all. Modern phones and computers offer several wireless ways to move files, and most of them take less than a minute once you know where to look.

The simplest option for a few files is the one you already use every day: messaging or email. Send the photo to yourself in a chat app, or attach it to an email and open it on your computer.

Use Your Phone and Computer Built-in Tools

Both Android and iPhone now have sharing features built in. Android phones can send files to Windows computers and Chromebooks with a nearby sharing feature, while iPhones can use AirDrop to send files to a Mac in seconds. These tools work over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, keep your files at full quality, and need no extra app. Make sure both devices are on the same Wi-Fi network, turn on Bluetooth if asked, and accept the transfer on the receiving device. For larger collections, it also pays to keep a backup habit, and our guide to backing up your photos and files shows a quick routine that protects everything you move.

If your phone and computer are different brands, a cloud folder is the easiest bridge. Drop files into a folder in Google Drive, OneDrive, or a similar service on your phone, and they appear on your computer a few moments later. Our comparison of the best free cloud storage services will help you pick one with enough free space for your needs.

Move Large Files Without the Wait

For videos and large folders, cloud uploads can feel slow, especially on a weak connection. In that case, try a direct Wi-Fi transfer app, which sends files straight from your phone to your computer over your local network without uploading them to the internet first. These apps usually show a web address or a code on your phone; you open it in your computer browser and download the files. It is fast, free, and your files never leave your home network.

Whichever method you choose, keep a few habits in mind. Once you have tried one wireless method, the cable becomes a backup rather than a daily necessity, and moving files between your devices feels as easy as sending a message.
image_alt: A hand holding a smartphone with a dark lock screen in the evening
author: The Edge Search

title: Best Apps for Scanning Documents with Your Phone
excerpt: Your phone camera can replace a scanner for receipts, forms, and notes. These apps turn photos into clean, shareable PDFs in minutes.
body_html:
A scanner used to be a bulky machine on a desk, but today the best scanner is the phone already in your pocket. With the right app, your camera can capture a receipt, a signed form, a handwritten note, or a page from a book, straighten the edges, sharpen the text, and save it as a clean PDF you can email or store.

The trick is that a scanning app does much more than take a photo. It detects the edges of the page automatically, corrects the perspective when you hold the phone at an angle, and boosts the contrast so the text reads clearly. Many apps can also recognise the text in the image, so you can search or copy words from a scan later.

What Makes a Good Scanning App

Start with the basics: automatic edge detection, a clear preview before you save, and an easy way to export as PDF or image. Batch scanning matters too, because scanning a ten-page contract one page at a time is tedious if the app makes you start over for each page. Look for apps that let you scan multiple pages into a single PDF, reorder pages, and retake a single page without losing the rest. If you are digitising a family archive rather than a single form, our guide to digitising old photos and documents at home covers the wider process, from lighting to storage.

Text recognition, often called OCR, is the feature that separates good apps from great ones. With it, a scanned receipt becomes searchable text, and a printed article becomes words you can copy into a note. If you scan sensitive documents, prefer an app that processes text on your device and lets you store files locally or in a cloud account you trust.

Scan Like a Pro With Your Phone

Good results start before you tap the shutter. Place the page on a flat surface with even light, avoid shadows from your hands or the phone, and hold the camera straight above the page. Dark text on white paper scans best, and a plain background helps the app find the edges.

Once a scan is saved as a PDF, it behaves like any other document: you can sign it, merge it with other pages, or send it straight to someone who needs it. Our roundup of the best free PDF tools shows how to edit, merge, and sign those files without paying. With one good scanning app and a few minutes of practice, your phone becomes a scanner that goes everywhere you do.

title: SIM Swap Attacks: How Criminals Steal Your Phone Number
excerpt: In a SIM swap attack, a criminal convinces your mobile carrier to move your number to their SIM. Here is how it works and how to stop it.
body_html:
Your phone number is more than a way to call you. It is also a key to your email, your bank, and your social media accounts, because so many services send login codes by text message. A SIM swap attack targets that key. A criminal tricks your mobile carrier into moving your number to a SIM card the criminal controls, and suddenly the codes meant for you go to them instead.

The attack usually starts with information about you. The criminal may gather your name, date of birth, and address from a data breach or from social media, then call your carrier pretending to be you and claim the phone was lost or stolen.

Why a Stolen Number Is So Dangerous

Once the attacker controls your number, password resets become easy. Many services let you reset a password with a code sent by text, so the attacker can request a reset for your email, get the code, and lock you out. From your email they can reach your bank, your shopping accounts, and your social media, often within an hour. Adding a second layer of protection helps a lot, and our guide to two-factor authentication shows how to turn it on in five minutes, ideally with an authenticator app rather than text messages.

The warning signs are worth knowing. If your phone suddenly loses signal for no reason, especially while you are in a place with good coverage, contact your carrier immediately. Unexpected password reset messages, alerts about logins you did not make, or a bank notification about a change you never requested are also red flags.

How to Protect Your Number

Start with your carrier. Ask it to add a PIN or a password to your account, so no one can request a SIM change without it, and ask whether it offers extra protection against SIM swaps. Then move your important accounts away from text-message codes. Authenticator apps generate codes on your phone without using your number, and security keys are stronger still. If the worst happens and an account is taken over, our recovery checklist on what to do if your account is hacked walks you through regaining control step by step.

Finally, limit the personal details you share online. The less a criminal can find about you, the harder it is to impersonate you to a carrier. Keep your number private where you can, use a separate number or email for public listings, and review your account security every few months. A stolen number is a frightening idea, but a carrier PIN and app-based codes make this attack much harder to pull off.

author: The Edge Search

title: Schema Markup Explained: Help Search Engines Understand Your Pages
excerpt: Schema markup is extra code that tells search engines what your page is about. It can earn richer results, like ratings and event details.
body_html:
Search engines are good at reading words, but they are not always sure what those words mean. Is 2027 a year, a price, or a model number? Is a name a person, a business, or a book? Schema markup answers those questions. It is a small block of extra code you add to a page that labels the important facts in a way search engines understand, such as this page is a recipe, it takes thirty minutes, and it has four hundred reviews.

That clarity can change how your page appears in search results. Pages with schema markup may earn rich results, the enhanced listings that show stars, prices, event dates, or cooking times right on the results page.

The Types of Schema Most Sites Should Know

You do not need every type of schema, just the ones that match your content. Articles and blog posts use Article schema, products use Product schema with price and availability, local businesses use LocalBusiness schema with address and opening hours, and events use Event schema with dates and location. Recipes, reviews, and frequently asked questions each have their own types too. Rich results are a powerful way to stand out, and our guide to featured snippets and People Also Ask explains how to win more search visibility with the content on the page itself.

The most common format is JSON-LD, a block of code placed in the head of the page that search engines can read without changing anything visitors see. Many content systems and SEO plugins can generate it for you, and you can test it with the free validation tools search engines provide.

Add Schema Without Breaking Your Site

Keep your markup simple and accurate. Only mark up facts that are actually visible on the page, keep prices and dates up to date, and do not add review stars unless the page really has reviews. After adding schema, use a testing tool to confirm there are no errors, and check the search console a few weeks later to see whether rich results are appearing. Schema sits alongside the technical side of SEO, so it also helps to know how search engines find your pages in the first place, as our guide to technical SEO basics explains.

Schema markup is not magic, and it will not rescue a weak page. But for a site with good content, it is one of the cheapest wins in SEO: a little extra code that helps search engines understand your pages and show them at their best. Add it to your most important pages first, validate it, and let the richer results do their work.
image_alt: Computer code and browser developer tools displayed on a dark screen
author: The Edge Search

title: AI Meeting Notes: Let Chatbots Summarise Your Calls
excerpt: AI meeting tools can turn a long call into a short summary with decisions and action items. Here is how to use them without missing details.
body_html:
Most meetings end the same way: everyone leaves with a different memory of what was decided, and the person who promised to write notes runs out of time. AI meeting tools fix that gap. They listen to the call, turn the speech into text, and then produce a short summary with the key points, the decisions made, and the tasks each person agreed to do.

These tools work with the video call apps most teams already use, and many of them join the meeting as a participant or record it with your permission. After the call, you receive the transcript and the summary, often organised by topic or speaker.

What AI Meeting Notes Do Well

The biggest win is accuracy about decisions. Human note-takers miss things when the discussion moves fast, but a transcript catches every word, and the summary can surface the exact moment a decision was made. This is especially useful for long meetings, for teams across time zones, and for anyone who could not attend live. A colleague who missed the call can read the summary and catch up without asking everyone to repeat themselves. The same idea applies to planning your day around meetings, and our look at AI voice assistants for daily planning shows what actually works when you let an assistant organise your schedule.

AI summaries also make follow-up easier. Instead of a vague note saying discuss the budget, you get a clear record: Sarah will send the revised budget by Friday. That clarity reduces the back-and-forth after meetings and gives the team a shared record everyone can check.

Use Them Carefully and Check the Output

AI summaries are not perfect. They can mishear names, confuse similar words, or invent a detail that was never said, especially when several people talk at once or the audio quality is poor. Always skim the summary before you share it, and fix any mistakes that change a decision or a deadline. For long calls, a good summary of the recording is only half the job; knowing how to get useful summaries of long material matters too, as our guide to how to get useful AI summaries explains.

Used with that care, AI meeting notes save real time. You can stay present in the conversation instead of scribbling, and still leave with a reliable record. Start with one regular meeting, compare the AI summary with your own notes for a week, and keep the tool only if it earns its place. For most busy teams, it does.

title: Robot Vacuums in 2027: Are They Worth It for Busy Homes?
excerpt: Robot vacuums promise clean floors without lifting a finger. Here is what they do well, where they struggle, and who should buy one.
body_html:
Robot vacuums have moved from a novelty to a normal household appliance. The latest models map your home, avoid cables and pet bowls, empty their own dustbins, and even mop hard floors, all while you are at work or cooking dinner.

The biggest change in recent years is navigation. Early robot vacuums bumped around randomly and missed spots, but modern models build a map of your home on the first run and then clean in neat rows.

Where Robot Vacuums Shine

Robot vacuums are at their best on hard floors and low-pile carpets, where they pick up dust, crumbs, and pet hair every day. That daily pass is the real benefit: floors never get as dirty as they do with a weekly clean, and homes with pets or small children notice the difference quickly. Scheduling a clean while you are out means coming home to tidy floors with no effort at all. They fit naturally into a connected home, and if you are building one, our smart home starter kit lists five devices that are actually useful alongside a robot vacuum.

Self-emptying docks are the feature most owners praise. Instead of emptying a small dustbin after every run, the vacuum empties itself into a bag in the dock that lasts a month or more.

Where They Struggle, and Who Should Buy One

Robot vacuums still struggle with thick carpets, stairs, and cluttered floors. Cables, socks, and small toys can tangle the brush or stop a run, so a quick tidy before cleaning helps a lot. They are also noisier than many people expect, and the dustbin bags and filters add a small running cost. If your home is mostly carpeted or has many steps and thresholds, a robot may disappoint you. Voice control and app scheduling make them easier to live with, and our review of smart speakers in 2027 covers the speakers that pair well with a robot vacuum for hands-free control.

So, are they worth it? For a busy home with hard floors or low carpets, pets, and a habit of daily mess, yes: the time saved adds up fast. For a small flat with thick carpet and little foot traffic, a good upright vacuum may be the better buy. If you decide to get one, choose a model with mapping, a self-emptying dock, and a dustbin you can clean easily, and give it a tidy floor to work with. It will not clean your whole home for you, but it will quietly handle the everyday dirt.

title: How to Make Your Phone Battery Last All Day
excerpt: Your phone battery does not have to die by dinner. These simple settings and habits can stretch a single charge through the whole day.
body_html:
Nothing is more annoying than watching your phone battery drop to ten percent in the middle of the afternoon, with hours still to go. The good news is that most battery problems are not caused by a faulty battery. They are caused by a bright screen, apps running in the background, and settings that quietly drain power all day.

Start with the screen, because it is usually the biggest drain on your battery. Lower the brightness to a comfortable level instead of leaving it at maximum, and turn on automatic brightness so the phone adjusts itself when you step indoors or outdoors.

Find the Apps That Drain Your Battery

Every phone has a battery settings page that shows which apps used the most power in the last day. Check it, and you will often find one or two surprises: a social media app refreshing in the background, a game you forgot was running, or a navigation app still tracking your location. A phone that is working hard in the background will also feel slower, and our guide to speeding up a slow computer shares the same idea: stop the hidden work you do not need and the device feels faster and lasts longer.

Also check your connections. Wi-Fi uses less power than mobile data when you are at home or in the office, while Bluetooth and location services add a small drain when they are left on all day. Low power mode, built into most phones, is a useful shortcut when your battery is running low: it dims the screen, pauses background activity, and can buy you several extra hours.

Habits That Keep Your Battery Healthy

How you charge matters as much as how you use the phone. Try to keep the battery between twenty and eighty percent most of the time, rather than charging it to full and draining it to empty every day. A phone that is several years old may also have a worn battery, and in that case a battery replacement is often cheaper than a new phone. If you are choosing a new handset, battery size and charging speed are worth comparing, and our roundup of the best budget smartphones in 2027 looks at what you get for less, including battery life.

None of these steps is difficult on its own, and together they make a real difference. Dim the screen, quiet the background apps, use low power mode when you need it, and charge with care. Do that, and your phone should still have charge left when the day ends, instead of giving up halfway through it.

author: The Edge Search

title: Best Free Project Management Tools for Small Teams
excerpt: Small teams do not need expensive software to stay organised. These project management tools cover tasks, deadlines, and teamwork without the price tag.
body_html:
Running a small team means juggling tasks, deadlines, and files across a handful of people, and a shared spreadsheet quickly turns into a mess. Free project management tools solve that problem by giving everyone one place to see what needs doing, who is doing it, and when it is due. The trick is picking a tool that matches how your team actually works, rather than the one with the longest feature list.

Start by listing what your team does every week. If most of your work is a simple flow from idea to done, a board-based tool will feel natural. If you juggle deadlines, dependencies, and different roles, you will want lists, timelines, and reminders. Also check how the tool handles files and chat, because a project board that cannot hold a document or a quick comment will push your team back to email. If your files live in several places at once, our comparison of free cloud storage can help you tidy that up first.

What to Look for in a Free Plan

Free plans are generous, but they all have limits, so read the small print before you commit. Check how many team members and projects the free tier allows, and whether it caps file uploads or activity history. A tool that is free for three people but charges for the fourth can surprise you as you grow. Also look for the basics that save time every day: due dates, checklists, labels, comments, and a mobile app that actually works. If your team still works with paper forms, apps that scan documents with your phone can feed the paperwork straight into your project board.

Integrations matter too. A tool that connects to your calendar, email, and chat app keeps updates in one place instead of scattered across tabs. Try the free plan on a real project for two weeks first.

The Best Free Options for Small Teams

Trello is the simplest starting point: cards on boards that you drag from to-do to done, with checklists and due dates on every card. Asana's free plan suits teams that want lists, timelines, and task assignments in one view. ClickUp packs the most features into its free tier, including docs and goals, though it can feel busy at first. Notion works well if your team wants notes, wikis, and tasks in a single workspace.

Whichever you choose, keep the setup simple. One board per project, clear task names, and a weekly habit of clearing done items will do more for your team than any premium feature. Start small, let the team shape the workflow, and upgrade only when a limit genuinely gets in the way.

title: How to Keep Your Location Private on Your Phone
excerpt: Your phone knows where you are, often down to the street. These settings and habits stop apps, photos, and advertisers from tracking your location.
body_html:
Your phone knows where you are, often down to the street corner, and it shares that information more widely than most people realise. Apps ask for your location, photos store it silently, and advertisers use it to build a picture of your daily routine. A few settings changes and small habits can cut most of the tracking without making your phone any less useful.

The biggest leak is location permission. Many apps ask for it on first launch, and it is easy to tap Allow without thinking. Go through your settings once and ask, for each app, whether it truly needs to know where you are. Removing permission from the apps that do not need it is the single most effective step you can take.

Tighten Location Permissions App by App

On an iPhone, open Settings, then Privacy and Security, then Location Services, and work through the list. Choose Never for apps that do not need location at all, and While Using the App for the ones that do. On Android, the same list lives under Settings, then Location, then App location permissions. Also switch off Precise Location where the option appears, and check the system services list, where features like location-based suggestions and ads quietly use your movements too.

Remember that location is not only about apps. Your photos carry it as well, stored as hidden data inside each image file. Before you share a photo taken at home or at your child's school, turn off location in the camera settings or strip it when you share. And think twice before checking in on social media: a public post that names a place also names the time you were there, as our guide to protecting your privacy on social media explains.

Stop Sharing Location Without Realising It

Several features share your location in the background. Google Maps Timeline keeps a history of everywhere you have been, and you can pause it or delete past visits in the app's settings. Apple's Find My and Google's location sharing are useful for family safety, but check who can actually see you and remove anyone who no longer needs access. The same goes for your web browser, which can hand your location to any site that asks, so set the permission to Ask every time.

Finally, remember that your phone number itself can be a way in. Criminals who take over a number can reset accounts tied to it, so it is worth understanding how SIM swap attacks steal your phone number and how to guard against them. Check your location settings every few months, because app updates can quietly turn old permissions back on.
image_alt: A hand holding a smartphone showing its lock screen
author: The Edge Search

title: How to Find and Fix Broken Links on Your Website
excerpt: Broken links frustrate visitors and waste search engine crawls. Here is how to find every dead link on your site and fix each one properly.
body_html:
A broken link is a small thing that causes real damage. A visitor clicks, lands on an error page, and quietly leaves. A search engine follows the same link, finds nothing, and slowly trusts your site a little less. The good news is that finding and fixing them is one of the simplest maintenance jobs in SEO, and it makes a visible difference to visitors.

Start with a full crawl of your site. Free tools like Screaming Frog will list every link it can follow and flag the ones that return an error, usually a 404. Google Search Console does the same job from Google's point of view: its Pages report shows which of your URLs are not found. Browser extensions can also check the links on a single page while you browse it. Export the list and fix the most-clicked broken links first.

How to Find Broken Links on Your Site

Do not forget the links you cannot see on a page. Your navigation menus, footer links, and old blog posts are the most common hiding places, and broken images count too, since a missing image is a broken link with a picture attached. Check links to other websites as well as your own pages: a resource you linked to five years ago may have moved or disappeared entirely. A regular check every few months keeps the list short, and it pairs well with a simple SEO audit of your own website, which covers the other basics in one pass.

When you find a broken link, note where it appears and where it was supposed to point. That context decides the fix.

How to Fix Them Without Losing Traffic

The best fix depends on what happened to the target page. If the page moved, set up a 301 redirect from the old address to the new one, so visitors and search engines land in the right place. If the page still exists under a slightly different address, simply update the link. If the page is gone for good, remove the link or replace it with a similar page that still helps the reader. Avoid redirecting everything to your homepage, because that confuses visitors more than an honest error page does.

After fixing, check that the redirects work and that the error pages are gone from your next crawl. Then keep your link structure healthy: when you add new pages, connect them properly, as our beginner's guide to internal linking shows. A site with no dead ends is easier to use, easier to crawl, and easier to trust.

title: AI Coding Assistants for Beginners: Write Code Without Experience
excerpt: AI coding assistants can write code from a plain-language description. Here is how beginners can use them to build things while learning how code works.
body_html:
You do not need years of experience to write working code any more. AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, Cursor, and Replit can turn a plain-language description into real, running code in seconds. Describe what you want, and the assistant suggests the code, fills in the gaps, and explains what each part does. That changes coding from a blank screen into a conversation.

These tools are not magic, and they are not a replacement for understanding. The skill is learning to ask clearly, check the result, and understand enough of what came back to know whether it does what you asked. Used that way, an AI assistant is a patient tutor that never gets tired of your questions.

How AI Coding Assistants Actually Work

Most assistants work in two ways. The first is autocomplete: as you type, the tool suggests the next lines, often completing a whole function before you finish the first one. The second is chat: you describe a feature in words, and the assistant writes the code for it, or explains code you paste in. Both work best when you give context, such as the programming language, what the code should do, and what should happen when something goes wrong. Clear, specific requests get far better results than vague ones, which is why learning to write better prompts helps with coding just as much as it helps with ordinary AI chat.

The assistant can also explain, debug, and improve code. Paste in an error message and ask what it means. Ask it to rewrite a messy function in a simpler way. Ask why it chose one approach over another. Each answer teaches you something, and over time you will find yourself needing the assistant less for simple tasks and more for genuinely hard ones.

A Beginner's First Project with an AI Assistant

Start small: a personal to-do page, a tip calculator, or a simple quiz. Describe the project in one paragraph, let the assistant build a first version, then run it and see what breaks. Fixing those small failures is where the learning happens. Read the code the assistant wrote, line by line, and ask it to explain any part you do not understand. If a suggestion looks odd, ask for a simpler version.

Keep your expectations honest. AI assistants can produce code that looks right but contains a subtle bug, so test everything and never paste in passwords or private data. As our guide to how AI assistants remember context explains, the assistant builds on what you have already told it, so a longer session with good context beats a dozen short, vague ones. Build something small, finish it, then build something slightly bigger.
